AlternativeReqPredicateError.description: An AlternativeReqPredicateError occurs when a cryptographic object does not satisfy a required security condition, specifically one that consists of a set of alternatives. CrySL rules may specify that a cryptographic object must fulfill a security property (e.g., a key must be generated securely before use). If this property and all relevant alternatives are missing or unverified, this error is reported. Such errors indicate that the cryptographic operation might not meet the required security guarantees, leading to potential vulnerabilities such as weak key material or improper algorithm usage.

examples.misuse:
This follow-up error occurs when none of the following predicates are fulfilled for the key given in the init method:
  • The key for the specified algorithm was properly generated.
  • The key is a properly generated public key.
  • The key is a properly generated private key.
Therefore, consider checking for issue tags involving the following classes:
  • java.security.Key (Key)
  • java.security.PublicKey (PublicKey)
  • java.security.PrivateKey (PrivateKey)

This follow-up error occurs when none of the following predicates are fulfilled when calling the getEncoded method:

  • javax.crypto.KeyGenerator (KeyGenerator)

  • java.security.PrivateKey (PrivateKey)

CallToError.description: A CallToError occurs when a required method call is missing in the usage of a cryptographic API. CrySL rules define mandatory method invocations that must occur when using a particular cryptographic object. If the expected method is not invoked, the security or functionality of the cryptographic operation may be compromised. This error often arises when a cryptographic object needs explicit initialization, but the developer fails to invoke the required method. Missing such calls may lead to improper configuration, weaker security guarantees, or even runtime exceptions when the API is used incorrectly.

examples.solution:

ConstraintError.description: A ConstraintError is triggered when a cryptographic API is used with parameters that do not comply with security constraints defined in the CrySL rule. These constraints can apply to algorithm selection, key sizes, padding schemes, or cryptographic modes. Such an error indicates that the provided argument violates predefined security policies, which could result in weak encryption, predictable cryptographic outputs, or even insecure configurations that attackers can exploit.

A ConstraintError was triggered due to the use of invalid parameters or transformations in the javax.crypto.Cipher API. This means the current usage violates the defined CONSTRAINTS in the CrySL specification.

Common violations include:
  • Using a key type that is incompatible with the specified transformation
  • Using an unsupported algorithm, mode, or padding
  • Missing or invalid init() calls
  • Calling updateAAD() when it's disallowed
  • Providing incorrect offset or length values that cause array index violations
  • Failing to call getIV() when required by the mode

the following constraints must be fulfilled:

examples._comment: BigInteger is class of java.math package which allows to work with numbers that are too big to fit in standard integer types like int. Cryptographic algorithm require very large prime numbers-often 2048 bits or more and regular int or long max out at 32 or 64bits.
examples.misuse:
Misuse: Using insecure DSA parameters that violate minimum bit-length constraints.

BigInteger p = new BigInteger("123456789"); // Too short
BigInteger q = new BigInteger("12345");
BigInteger g = new BigInteger("67890"); // Too short
DSAParameterSpec spec = new DSAParameterSpec(p, q, g);

This creates a DSAParameterSpec with parameters that do not meet security requirements (e.g., p < 2048 bits).
examples.solution:
Solution: Use strong DSA parameters that meet the minimum 2048-bit requirement.

// Example of generating secure parameters using KeyPairGenerator
KeyPairGenerator keyGen = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("DSA");
keyGen.initialize(2048);
KeyPair pair = keyGen.generateKeyPair();
DSAParams dsaParams = ((DSAPublicKey) pair.getPublic()).getParams();
DSAParameterSpec spec = new DSAParameterSpec(dsaParams.getP(), dsaParams.getQ(), dsaParams.getG());

This ensures that the parameters used in DSAParameterSpec are secure and conform to modern cryptographic standards.

ForbiddenMethodError.description: A ForbiddenMethodError occurs when an explicitly restricted method is invoked in cryptographic operations. Some methods are banned due to known security vulnerabilities or deprecated functionality. When this error is reported, it means that the method being used is considered insecure or does not comply with best practices. Ignoring this error may lead to weak encryption, insecure randomness, or potential exploitation of deprecated algorithms.

HardCodedError.description: A HardCodedError is reported when sensitive cryptographic values, such as encryption keys, passwords, IVs (Initialization Vectors), or salts, are hardcoded into the source code. Hardcoded values expose cryptographic secrets to attackers, making them easy to extract via static analysis, reverse engineering, or memory dumps. This error serves as a warning that sensitive cryptographic parameters should be dynamically generated and stored securely to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of cryptographic operations.

ImpreciseValueExtractionError.description: An ImpreciseValueExtractionError is triggered when the analysis tool cannot precisely determine the value of a cryptographic parameter at runtime. This typically happens when cryptographic values (such as encryption modes or key sizes) are computed dynamically or retrieved from an external source, making them difficult to validate statically. This error highlights potential security risks where cryptographic operations might unknowingly use insecure or unpredictable values. It suggests that cryptographic parameters should be explicitly defined and verifiable.

IncompleteOperationError.description: An IncompleteOperationError is reported when a cryptographic operation is not fully completed as expected. CrySL rules define a specific order of operations (e.g., an encryption process requires initialization before performing encryption, followed by finalization). If a required step is missing, the cryptographic process may remain incomplete, potentially leading to unencrypted data, insecure partial outputs, or unexpected runtime failures. This error ensures that cryptographic workflows are executed in their entirety to maintain security.

InstanceOfError.description: An InstanceOfError occurs when an object used in a cryptographic operation does not match the expected type. CrySL rules enforce type constraints on cryptographic objects (e.g., a Cipher object might require a SecretKey, but a PublicKey is provided instead). This error prevents incorrect type usage that could lead to runtime failures, security vulnerabilities, or unintentional misconfiguration of cryptographic components.

NeverTypeOfError.description: A NeverTypeOfError occurs when a parameter is of a type that is explicitly disallowed.

NoCallToError.description: A NoCallToError is triggered when a method is explicitly prohibited in a cryptographic usage pattern, yet it has been invoked. CrySL rules may specify that certain method calls should not occur under specific conditions, such as restricting init() for certain algorithms that do not require explicit initialization. This error signals that the cryptographic implementation does not follow secure guidelines and may introduce security weaknesses.

SecretKey sharedKey = keAgreement.generateSecret(symmetricKeyAlgorithm);
examples.solution:
Instead use 
byte[] sharedSecretBuffer = keyAgreement.generateSecret();
or 
byte[] sharedSecretBuffer = new byte[1024];
generateSecret(sharedSecretBuffer, offset);

RequiredPredicateError.description: A RequiredPredicateError occurs when a cryptographic object does not satisfy a required security condition. CrySL rules may specify that a cryptographic object must fulfill a security property (e.g., a key must be generated securely before use). If this property is missing or unverified, this error is reported. Such errors indicate that the cryptographic operation might not meet the required security guarantees, leading to potential vulnerabilities such as weak key material or improper algorithm usage.

TypestateError.description: A TypestateError is reported when cryptographic operations occur in an incorrect sequence. CrySL rules define a strict ordering of method calls (e.g., an object must be initialized before use). If the operations are performed in an unexpected order, the cryptographic process may become unreliable or insecure. This error ensures that cryptographic APIs are used in their intended sequence, preventing unintended behavior or security gaps in encryption, decryption, and key management.
